title: The Columbian Exchange
summary: After Columbus's 1492 voyage, plants, animals and diseases crossed the Atlantic in both directions. American crops such as maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cassava, chili peppers and tobacco spread across Afro-Eurasia, while wheat, rice, sugar cane, horses, cattle, pigs and sheep transformed the Americas. Old World diseases such as smallpox, first recorded in the Americas in 1518, together with war, enslavement and exploitation, cut the Indigenous population of the Americas (perhaps around 50 million before contact, though estimates vary widely) by an estimated 80 to 95 percent.
why: The exchange reshaped diets, farming and populations across the world: cassava became Africa's most important food crop, while maize, potatoes and sweet potatoes fed population growth in Asia and Europe, while the peoples of the Americas suffered a demographic catastrophe.
also: Silver flowed the other way: the Cerro Rico at Potosí (in today's Bolivia), discovered in 1545 and worked by Indigenous forced labour under the mita system, was the Spanish Empire's main source of silver until the 18th century, and some of it crossed the Pacific on the Manila galleons to buy Asian goods.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Population history of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas

title: Luther's Ninety-five Theses and the Reformation
summary: On 31 October 1517 the theologian Martin Luther sent his Ninety-five Theses, an attack on the sale of indulgences, to the Archbishop of Mainz; by tradition he also posted them on the door of All Saints' Church in Wittenberg. Several hundred printed copies circulated in Germany that year, and Luther's challenge to papal authority grew into the Protestant Reformation, carried further by reformers such as Huldrych Zwingli and John Calvin and, in England, under Henry VIII.
why: The Reformation split Western Christianity into Catholic and Protestant churches, used the printing press to spread religious writing in everyday languages, and fed the European wars of religion, which killed an estimated 7 to 17 million people.

title: First circumnavigation of the Earth
place: Sanlúcar de Barrameda, Spain (departure and return port)
summary: Five ships and about 270 men left Spain on 20 September 1519 under the Portuguese navigator Ferdinand Magellan, seeking a western route to the Spice Islands (the Moluccas). The fleet entered the strait now named after Magellan on 1 November 1520 and crossed the Pacific in 98 days, but Magellan was killed fighting Lapu-Lapu's forces at Mactan in the Philippines in April 1521. Juan Sebastián Elcano brought the last ship, the Victoria, home around Africa on 6 September 1522 with just 18 of the original crew aboard.
why: The voyage, the first by Europeans across the Pacific, revealed the vast size of that ocean and proved that ships could sail around the world by a western sea route.

title: Suleiman the Magnificent and the Ottoman zenith
summary: Suleiman I, sultan from 1520 to 1566, had the longest reign of any Ottoman ruler. He took Belgrade in 1521 and Rhodes in 1522, broke the Kingdom of Hungary at Mohács in 1526, besieged Vienna in 1529, annexed Iraq in wars with Safavid Iran, and built a fleet that dominated the seas from the Mediterranean to the Persian Gulf. His chief architect, Mimar Sinan, is credited with over 300 buildings, including the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul.
why: His reign marked the peak of Ottoman power and culture, ruling at least 25 million subjects, while the failed siege of Vienna set the limit of the empire's advance into central Europe.

title: Fall of Tenochtitlan
summary: Hernán Cortés reached the Aztec (Mexica) capital Tenochtitlan in November 1519 with a small Spanish force and a far larger army of Indigenous allies, above all Tlaxcaltec warriors. After the Spaniards were driven from the city in 1520, smallpox killed an estimated 40 percent of its roughly 200,000 people, and the Spanish-led coalition besieged the island city until it surrendered on 13 August 1521 and its last ruler, Cuauhtémoc, was captured.
why: The fall of the most powerful state in Mesoamerica founded New Spain, governed from Mexico City on the site of Tenochtitlan, and opened the way to Spanish rule over much of the Americas.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire

title: Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire
summary: On 16 November 1532, 168 Spanish soldiers under Francisco Pizarro, with Indigenous auxiliaries, ambushed the Sapa Inca Atahualpa in the main square of Cajamarca, killing thousands of his unarmed attendants and taking him prisoner. The Inca Empire, by far the largest of the great pre-Columbian civilisations, had already been weakened by epidemics and by a civil war between Atahualpa and his brother Huáscar. Atahualpa paid a ransom but was executed in July 1533, and Inca resistance continued until 1572.
why: The conquest brought the Andes under Spanish rule as the Viceroyalty of Peru and launched further Spanish campaigns into present-day Chile and Colombia.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire

title: Copernicus puts the Sun at the centre
place: Frombork, Royal Prussia (now Poland), where Copernicus is buried
summary: In 1543, shortly before his death on 24 May, the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus published De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres), printed in Nuremberg. The book replaced Ptolemy's Earth-centred system, accepted since ancient times, with a model that placed the Sun at the centre of the universe.
why: It began the Copernican Revolution: once Johannes Kepler and Galileo Galilei supplied supporting evidence half a century later, the Sun-centred model became a cornerstone of the Scientific Revolution.
also: Acceptance was slow: by one count, sixty years after publication only about 15 astronomers in all of Europe supported Copernicus's system.

title: Akbar and the Mughal high point
summary: The Mughal Empire was founded in 1526, when Babur, a Timurid prince from Central Asia, defeated Sultan Ibrahim Lodi of Delhi at the First Battle of Panipat. Babur's grandson Akbar, emperor from 1556 to 1605, extended it over much of the Indian subcontinent, built a centralised administration, won the support of non-Muslim subjects by abolishing the sectarian jizya tax, and drew scholars, poets and holy men of many faiths to his courts, including his new capital at Fatehpur Sikri (1571–1585).
why: Mughal India was one of the world's great manufacturing economies, producing about a quarter of world industrial output until 1750, and its architecture culminated in the Taj Mahal under Akbar's grandson Shah Jahan.
also: The empire reached its greatest extent under Aurangzeb (d. 1707), then broke up, and was formally dissolved by the British after the Indian Rebellion of 1857.

title: The Atlantic slave trade
place: Atlantic coast of West and Central Africa (pin: Luanda, Angola)
summary: From the 16th century until well into the 19th, European and American traders bought captives from West and Central African merchants and states and shipped them across the Atlantic on the 'Middle Passage' to be sold into slavery in Brazil, the Caribbean and the rest of the Americas. An estimated 12.5 million people were carried off from Africa, of whom about 10.7 million survived the voyage.
why: In the first three centuries after Columbus far more Africans than Europeans crossed to the Americas, and the trade and the slavery it fed shaped the populations, economies and societies of the Atlantic world.
also: Queen Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba (in present-day Angola) fought Portuguese expansion in the 17th century. Britain banned its slave trade in 1807 and the United States soon followed, but slavery itself lasted in Brazil until 1888.

title: The Qing take Beijing
summary: In April 1644 Beijing fell to the rebel army of Li Zicheng, and the last Ming emperor, the Chongzhen Emperor, hanged himself in the imperial garden outside the Forbidden City. Manchu forces, aided by the defecting Ming general Wu Sangui, defeated Li at Shanhai Pass and entered Beijing in June 1644, beginning the Qing dynasty's rule over China; Ming loyalists held out in the south and on Taiwan until 1683.
why: The Qing, China's last imperial dynasty, ruled until 1912, controlled more territory than any earlier Chinese dynasty and assembled the territorial base of modern China.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Transition from Ming to Qing

title: Thirty Years' War and the Peace of Westphalia
summary: Rooted in the religious divisions of the Holy Roman Empire that followed the Reformation, and in disputes over imperial authority, the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) drew in Austria, Spain, Sweden, France and many German states. An estimated 4.5 to 8 million soldiers and civilians died from battle, famine or disease, and parts of Germany lost more than half their population. Treaties signed at Münster and Osnabrück in October 1648, together called the Peace of Westphalia, ended the war; earlier that year Spain and the Dutch Republic had made peace at Münster, ending the Eighty Years' War.
why: Many international-relations scholars trace the principle of sovereign states that do not interfere in one another's internal affairs ('Westphalian sovereignty') to this settlement, though some historians argue that reading was a later invention.

title: Newton's Principia
place: London (published under the Royal Society's imprimatur)
summary: Isaac Newton's Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), approved by the Royal Society in July 1686 and published in 1687, set out his laws of motion and his law of universal gravitation. With one set of mathematical principles Newton explained Kepler's laws of planetary motion, the paths of comets, the tides and irregularities in the Moon's motion.
why: The Principia became the mathematical foundation of classical mechanics and is generally considered one of the most important works in the history of science; the Enlightenment is sometimes dated from its publication.

title: Glorious Revolution and the Bill of Rights
summary: In November 1688 the Catholic King James II of England was deposed after an invasion by his Dutch nephew and son-in-law, William of Orange, who then ruled jointly with James's daughter Mary II. The Bill of Rights, given royal assent on 16 December 1689, barred Catholics from the throne, forbade taxation or a peacetime standing army without Parliament's consent, and set out rights including free elections, regular parliaments, freedom of debate in Parliament and protection from cruel and unusual punishment.
why: It established that the Crown must govern with the consent of Parliament, and the Bill became one of the models for the United States Bill of Rights, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the European Convention on Human Rights.

title: The Enlightenment and the Encyclopédie
summary: The Enlightenment, an intellectual movement that emerged in Western and Central Europe in the late 17th century and peaked in the 18th, championed reason, evidence and the scientific method, and promoted individual liberty, religious tolerance, progress and natural rights. Its landmark was the Encyclopédie, edited by Denis Diderot (with Jean le Rond d'Alembert until 1759) and published in France from 1751 to 1772: 28 volumes with some 71,818 articles, which Diderot hoped would 'change the way people think'.
why: Enlightenment arguments for constitutional government, natural rights and the separation of church and state were a key inspiration for the American and French revolutions and remain foundations of modern democracy.
also: Leading figures included John Locke, Voltaire, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, David Hume, Adam Smith, Benjamin Franklin and Immanuel Kant.

title: The Seven Years' War
summary: Fought mainly between Britain and Prussia on one side and France and Austria, with Russia, Spain, Sweden and others, on the other, the Seven Years' War spread from Europe to North America, the Caribbean, West Africa, India and the Philippines. Britain's victories included Plassey in Bengal (23 June 1757) and the Plains of Abraham outside Quebec (13 September 1759); in the 1763 Treaty of Paris France ceded Canada and its other North American lands east of the Mississippi to Britain, and Louisiana to Spain. By one compilation of national estimates, the armies of the main belligerents lost roughly 900,000 dead.
why: The war made Britain the leading colonial power in North America and India, where the East India Company's victory at Plassey began its rule over Bengal.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Battle of the Plains of Abraham

title: Watt's steam engine and the Industrial Revolution
summary: Beginning in Great Britain around 1760, the Industrial Revolution moved production from hand methods to machines driven by water and steam, and brought the mechanised factory system, first in textiles: Richard Arkwright patented his water frame in 1769. That year James Watt also patented a separate condenser that made steam engines far more efficient than Thomas Newcomen's 1712 design; built commercially by Watt and Matthew Boulton from 1776, his engines used about half as much coal for the same power, and from 1781 could turn machinery with rotary motion.
why: Economic historians regard the Industrial Revolution as one of the most important events in human history, comparable to the adoption of farming: it set off an unprecedented rise in output and population and had spread to continental Europe and the United States by about 1840.

title: American Revolution and independence
summary: Quarrels between Britain and its Thirteen Colonies turned to war in April 1775. On 4 July 1776 the Second Continental Congress, meeting in Philadelphia, adopted the Declaration of Independence, drafted chiefly by Thomas Jefferson, which proclaimed that 'all men are created equal'. With French, Spanish and Dutch support, George Washington's Continental Army won a decisive victory at Yorktown in 1781, and Britain recognised American independence in the Treaty of Paris of 3 September 1783.
why: The revolution created the United States as a republic founded on Enlightenment ideas of natural rights and government by consent, and its Declaration has become one of the most circulated, reprinted and influential documents in history.

sources.title: Wikipedia: United States Declaration of Independence
US National Archives: Declaration of Independence

title: The First Fleet reaches Australia
summary: Eleven British ships under Captain Arthur Phillip, carrying over 1,400 convicts, marines, sailors and officials, reached Botany Bay in January 1788 and settled instead at Sydney Cove in Port Jackson on 26 January, founding the penal Colony of New South Wales. Aboriginal Australians had lived on the continent for 50,000 to 65,000 years; the local Eora people met the newcomers with curiosity and suspicion, and an outbreak of smallpox in April 1789 killed about half the Aboriginal population of the Sydney region.
why: It began the British colonisation of Australia, which brought disease, violent conflict and the dispossession of Aboriginal peoples from their lands; 26 January is still marked as Australia Day.
also: In New Zealand, the Treaty of Waitangi between the British Crown and Māori chiefs (rangatira), first signed on 6 February 1840, is increasingly recognised as a founding document of the country; its English and Māori texts differ, and their meaning is still debated.

title: The French Revolution
summary: Amid financial crisis and widespread distress, the Estates General met in May 1789 for the first time since 1614; the Third Estate broke away to form a National Assembly, and on 14 July crowds in Paris stormed the Bastille fortress. The Assembly abolished feudalism and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen; the monarchy was replaced by a republic in September 1792, Louis XVI was executed in January 1793, and after the Reign of Terror the Revolution ended when Napoleon Bonaparte seized power on 9 November 1799.
why: Many of its ideas are considered fundamental principles of liberal democracy, and the wars that grew out of it reshaped Europe.

title: The Haitian Revolution
summary: On 21 August 1791 enslaved Africans rose in revolt in Saint-Domingue, France's most profitable colony, which in 1789 produced 60 percent of the world's coffee. Through 13 years of war and shifting alliances, including British and Spanish interventions and a large French expedition sent by Napoleon in 1802, the rebels prevailed; their foremost general, the formerly enslaved Toussaint Louverture, died in a French prison in 1803, and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, who led the final campaign, declared Haiti independent at Gonaïves on 1 January 1804.
why: Haiti became the first independent nation in Latin America and the first post-colonial state founded and ruled by formerly enslaved people, and its revolution's effects on slavery were felt throughout the Americas.

title: Napoleonic Wars and Waterloo
summary: From 1803 Napoleon's France fought a series of coalitions of European powers and dominated most of the continent, until the failed invasion of Russia in 1812 and defeat in 1814 sent him into exile on Elba. Returning to power in March 1815, he was beaten for the last time on 18 June 1815 near Waterloo by the Duke of Wellington's British-led army and Gebhard von Blücher's Prussians, and abdicated four days later. Estimates of military deaths across the wars run from about 2.5 million to as many as 5 million, alongside many civilian victims.
why: The Congress of Vienna redrew Europe's borders, and Britain emerged as the world's foremost naval and economic power for the rest of the 19th century.

title: Latin American independence
summary: Napoleon's invasion of Spain in 1808 broke the authority of the Spanish Crown, and from 1810 juntas and revolts across Spanish America turned into wars of independence. Simón Bolívar led what are now Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Peru and Bolivia to independence and José de San Martín led the armies of the south, until Antonio José de Sucre's victory at Ayacucho on 9 December 1824 secured the independence of Peru and the rest of Spanish South America. Mexico's war (1810–1821) ended in independence, and Brazil declared independence from Portugal on 7 September 1822.
why: By 1826 Spain had lost its mainland American empire, keeping only Cuba and Puerto Rico until 1898, and new independent states took shape from Mexico to Argentina and Chile.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Spanish American wars of independence

title: The first inter-city railway
summary: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway, built by George Stephenson and opened on 15 September 1830, was the world's first inter-city railway and the first to rely entirely on steam locomotives, with double track, signalling and timetabled services. Its engines were chosen at the 1829 Rainhill trials, where the Stephensons' Rocket was the only locomotive to complete the course, and its opening day was marred when the MP William Huskisson was killed on the line.
why: Its financial success set off railway building across Britain in the 1830s, and from the 1840s railways largely replaced canals, carrying people and goods faster and cheaper than ever before.

title: The Opium Wars
summary: When the Qing official Lin Zexu forced British merchants at Guangzhou to hand over some 1,420 tonnes of opium and destroyed it at Humen in June 1839, Britain went to war to win compensation and open China to trade. British victories forced the Treaty of Nanjing (29 August 1842), which ceded Hong Kong Island, opened five treaty ports and imposed an indemnity; in the Second Opium War (1856–1860) Britain and France captured Beijing, burned the Old Summer Palace and forced the legalisation of the opium trade.
why: Chinese nationalists later counted 1839 as the start of a 'century of humiliation' under unequal treaties, and many historians date modern Chinese history from it.
also: The weakened Qing also faced the Taiping Rebellion (1850–1864), the deadliest civil war in history, in which an estimated 20 to 30 million people died.

title: Indian Rebellion of 1857
summary: On 10 May 1857 Indian soldiers (sepoys) of the British East India Company's army mutinied at Meerut; rebels quickly reached Delhi, where the 81-year-old Mughal ruler Bahadur Shah Zafar was declared Emperor of Hindustan, and the revolt spread through other regiments and civilian uprisings across the upper Gangetic plain and central India. British forces stormed Delhi in September 1857 and defeated the last major rebel army at Gwalior on 20 June 1858.
why: The rebellion led to the dissolution of the East India Company and, under the Government of India Act 1858, to direct rule of India by the British Crown; the last Mughal emperor was exiled and the dynasty ended.

title: Darwin's On the Origin of Species
place: Down House, Downe, Kent (England), Darwin's home
summary: Published on 24 November 1859, Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species argued that populations evolve over generations through natural selection and that the diversity of life arose by common descent, through a branching pattern of evolution. Darwin drew on evidence gathered on the voyage of HMS Beagle in the 1830s and on two decades of later research, and was spurred to publish after receiving a paper from Alfred Russel Wallace, who had reached similar ideas, in June 1858.
why: The book is considered the foundation of evolutionary biology.

sources.title: Wikipedia: On the Origin of Species

title: American Civil War
place: Fort Sumter, Charleston, South Carolina (where the war began)
summary: After Abraham Lincoln, who opposed the expansion of slavery, won the 1860 election, Southern slave states seceded to form the Confederacy, and the war began when Confederate forces bombarded Fort Sumter on 12 April 1861. Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation of 1 January 1863 declared more than 3.5 million enslaved people in Confederate territory free; General Robert E. Lee surrendered at Appomattox Court House on 9 April 1865, and the Thirteenth Amendment banned slavery throughout the United States from December 1865.
why: The deadliest war in US history, it left an estimated 700,000 soldiers dead, preserved the Union and freed four million African Americans from slavery.

title: Meiji Restoration
summary: The arrival of the US Perry Expedition in 1853 and the unequal treaties that followed undermined the Tokugawa shogunate, which had ruled Japan since 1603. On 3 January 1868 an alliance led by the Satsuma and Chōshū domains restored political power to the young Emperor Meiji; Tokugawa resistance was defeated in the Boshin War, and Edo was renamed Tokyo, where the emperor took up residence in 1869.
why: The new government dismantled the shogunal system and set Japan on a course of rapid industrialisation and Westernisation, adopting Western ideas, production methods and technology.

title: Berlin Conference and the Scramble for Africa
summary: Organised by German chancellor Otto von Bismarck at the request of King Leopold II of Belgium, the Berlin Conference met from 15 November 1884 to 26 February 1885, when fourteen countries signed the General Act regulating European colonisation and trade in Africa, including a common framework for recognising claims backed by 'effective occupation'. As late as the 1870s Europeans controlled about 10 percent of Africa, mostly near the coasts; by 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia remained outside European control.
why: The conference gave international legal backing to a rapid wave of European claims, and the colonial states carved out in the following decades became the framework from which most modern African countries emerged.

title: Battle of Adwa
summary: On 1 March 1896 the army of Emperor Menelik II, estimated at 73,000 to over 100,000 men and mostly armed with modern rifles bought from France and Russia, routed an Italian colonial force under General Oreste Baratieri that was trying to impose a protectorate on Ethiopia after a dispute over the Treaty of Wuchale. Over 6,000 Italian and colonial troops were killed and about 3,800 captured, while Ethiopian losses are estimated at 4,000 to 7,000 killed; Italy was forced to recognise Ethiopia's sovereignty in the Treaty of Addis Ababa.
why: Adwa kept Ethiopia independent through the Scramble for Africa, and the victory became a rallying point for later African nationalists and the Pan-African movement.
also: Ethiopia remained independent until Fascist Italy occupied it in 1936; Italian rule there ended during World War II.

title: World War I
place: Latin Bridge, Sarajevo (Bosnia and Herzegovina), site of the assassination
summary: On 28 June 1914 the Bosnian Serb student Gavrilo Princip assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, in Sarajevo; Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia, and within weeks Europe's alliance system had pulled the great powers into war between the Allies (the Entente) and the Central Powers. Machine guns, artillery, poison gas, aircraft and tanks made it one of the deadliest conflicts in history, with 15 to 22 million deaths, before the armistice of 11 November 1918.
why: The war destroyed the Russian, German, Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman empires, and the peace settlements that followed, including the Treaty of Versailles, left unresolved tensions that helped cause World War II.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand

title: Russian Revolution
summary: Amid military defeats and bread shortages in World War I, the February Revolution of 1917 forced Tsar Nicholas II to abdicate on 15 March (New Style) and ended the monarchy. On 7 November (25 October, Old Style) Vladimir Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in Petrograd, storming the Winter Palace, seat of the Provisional Government; after victory in the Russian Civil War they founded the Soviet Union on 30 December 1922.
why: Lenin's government created the world's first constitutionally communist state, and the Soviet Union's rivalry with the West shaped much of the 20th century.

title: The 1918 influenza pandemic
place: Haskell County, Kansas (earliest probable recorded cases)
summary: An H1N1 influenza virus caused an exceptionally deadly pandemic at the end of World War I and after; the earliest probable cases were documented in Haskell County, Kansas, in March 1918, though the virus's geographic origin is still uncertain. In two years an estimated 500 million people, nearly a third of the world's population, were infected, and estimates of deaths range from 17 million to 50 million, possibly as high as 100 million, with unusually high mortality among young adults.
why: It was one of the deadliest pandemics in history; it was misleadingly called 'Spanish flu' because wartime censors suppressed news elsewhere while newspapers in neutral Spain reported it freely.

title: Wall Street Crash and the Great Depression
place: New York Stock Exchange, Wall Street, New York City
summary: After a speculative boom, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell nearly 13 percent on Black Monday, 28 October 1929, and nearly 12 percent the next day, and had lost almost half its value by mid-November. The crash opened the Great Depression: between 1929 and 1932 world GDP fell by an estimated 15 percent, US unemployment reached 25 percent by 1933 and about 9,000 of the country's 25,000 banks failed, while tariffs such as the 1930 Smoot–Hawley Act helped collapse world trade.
why: The Depression brought new government intervention in the economy, such as Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal, and helped fascist movements, including the Nazis in Germany, rise to power.

sources.title: Federal Reserve History: Stock Market Crash of 1929

title: World War II
summary: World War II began on 1 September 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded Poland and Britain and France declared war on Germany; the Soviet Union invaded Poland from the east in mid-September, and Japan had been at war with China since 1937. Fought between the Allies and the Axis powers and involving nearly every country, it ended with Germany's surrender on 8 May 1945 and Japan's on 2 September 1945. It was the deadliest conflict in history: an estimated 60 to 75 million people died, most of them civilians.
why: The United States and the Soviet Union emerged as rival superpowers, setting the stage for the Cold War, while Europe's weakened powers began to lose their colonies in Africa and Asia.

title: The Holocaust
summary: From 1941 to 1945 Nazi Germany and its collaborators systematically murdered around six million Jews, about two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population, in mass shootings across Eastern Europe and in the gas chambers of extermination camps in occupied Poland. At the Auschwitz complex, the deadliest killing centre, at least 1.1 million people were killed, about a million of them Jews, before Soviet troops liberated it on 27 January 1945.
why: The Holocaust was state-sponsored mass murder on an unprecedented scale; the Nazi regime also killed Roma and Sinti, disabled people, Soviet prisoners of war and millions of other civilians.

sources.title: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia: Documenting Numbers of Victims of the Holocaust and Nazi Persecution

title: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
summary: On 6 August 1945 a US B-29 bomber dropped 'Little Boy', a uranium bomb, on Hiroshima, and three days later 'Fat Man', a plutonium bomb, on Nagasaki. By the end of 1945 the bombings had killed an estimated 150,000 to 246,000 people, most of them civilians. Japan announced its surrender on 15 August, six days after Nagasaki and the Soviet Union's declaration of war and invasion of Manchuria, and signed the instrument of surrender on 2 September.
why: They remain the only uses of nuclear weapons in an armed conflict, and they opened the nuclear age.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki

title: The United Nations is founded
place: San Francisco, USA (where the UN Charter was signed)
summary: Delegates of 50 countries met in San Francisco from 25 April to 26 June 1945 to draft the Charter of the United Nations, which they signed on 26 June; it came into force on 24 October 1945 after ratification by China, France, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, the United States and a majority of the other signatories. Succeeding the League of Nations, the UN was built around a General Assembly of all members, a Security Council in which those five powers hold permanent seats, and an International Court of Justice.
why: With 193 member states today it is the world's largest international organisation, and in 1948 its General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

sources.title: United Nations: History of the UN
Wikipedia: Charter of the United Nations

title: Indian independence and Partition
summary: At midnight on 14–15 August 1947 British rule in India ended and two independent dominions, India and Pakistan, came into existence under the Indian Independence Act. The provinces of Punjab and Bengal were divided according to Muslim or non-Muslim majorities, and Partition displaced 12 to 20 million people along religious lines amid communal violence whose death toll is estimated at 200,000 to 2 million.
why: Partition created the states that are today India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, and the contested accession of the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir became a lasting source of conflict between India and Pakistan.

title: People's Republic of China proclaimed
summary: After the Chinese Communist Party defeated Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists in the civil war that resumed in full in 1946, Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China in Tiananmen Square on 1 October 1949. The Nationalist government of the Republic of China retreated to Taiwan.
why: Communist rule brought sweeping social change to China, and the division between the People's Republic and the government on Taiwan that began in 1949 persists today.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Proclamation of the People's Republic of China

title: Korean War
summary: Korea, a Japanese colony for 35 years, was divided at the 38th parallel into Soviet and US occupation zones in 1945, and rival governments formed in 1948. On 25 June 1950 North Korea invaded the South; a US-led United Nations force came to the South's aid and China and the Soviet Union backed the North, and after two years of attritional fighting an armistice signed on 27 July 1953 created a 4-kilometre-wide Demilitarized Zone along the front line.
why: The war caused around one million military deaths and an estimated 1.5 to 3 million civilian deaths, and left Korea divided under an armistice that has never been replaced by a peace treaty.

title: Vietnam War
summary: After the First Indochina War ended French rule, Vietnam was divided between the communist North, backed by the Soviet Union and China, and the South, backed by the United States. Direct US military involvement escalated from 1965 and peaked in 1969; US forces withdrew in 1973, North Vietnamese forces captured Saigon on 30 April 1975, and the country was reunified in 1976. Estimates of Vietnamese soldiers and civilians killed range from about 970,000 to 3 million, and some 275,000–310,000 Cambodians, 20,000–62,000 Laotians and 58,220 US service members also died.
why: Both a war of national liberation and a Cold War proxy war, it spilled into Laos and Cambodia, and all three countries ended up under communist governments.

title: The Year of Africa
summary: After Ghana became independent from Britain on 6 March 1957, decolonisation swept the continent, and in 1960 alone seventeen African countries won independence: fourteen from France, two from Britain (Somalia and Nigeria, Africa's most populous country) and one from Belgium (the Congo). The process was often violent, as in the Algerian War (1954–1962) and the Congo Crisis that followed Congolese independence.
why: Between the mid-1950s and 1976 the colonial states created in the Scramble for Africa gave way to independent nations, and Africa emerged as a major force in the United Nations.

title: Cuban Missile Crisis
summary: On 14 October 1962 a US U-2 spy plane photographed Soviet nuclear missile sites being built in Cuba, and President John F. Kennedy imposed a naval 'quarantine' of the island on 22 October. After 13 days of confrontation, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev announced on 28 October that the missiles would be removed, in return for a US pledge not to invade Cuba and a secret US promise to withdraw its Jupiter missiles from Turkey.
why: Widely considered the closest the Cold War came to full-scale nuclear war, the crisis led to a Moscow–Washington hotline and a treaty banning atmospheric nuclear tests.

sources.title: Office of the Historian (US State Department): The Cuban Missile Crisis, October 1962

title: Apollo 11: humans on the Moon
summary: Launched on a Saturn V rocket from Kennedy Space Center on 16 July 1969, Apollo 11 carried Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins and Buzz Aldrin to the Moon. On 20 July Armstrong and Aldrin landed the lunar module Eagle in the Sea of Tranquility while Collins orbited in the command module Columbia; Armstrong became the first human to walk on the Moon, and the crew returned to Earth on 24 July with 21.5 kg of lunar material.
why: The landing was the culmination of the US–Soviet Space Race and fulfilled President Kennedy's 1961 challenge to land a man on the Moon before the end of the decade.

title: China's reform and opening-up
summary: Two years after Mao Zedong's death, the Chinese Communist Party, guided by Deng Xiaoping, launched 'reform and opening-up' on 18 December 1978, gradually opening the economy to markets and foreign investment. Shenzhen, on the border with Hong Kong, was made a special economic zone on 1 May 1980 and grew from a largely rural area into a global metropolis; China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001.
why: Between 1978 and 2018 China reduced extreme poverty by 800 million people, became the world's leading manufacturing power and in 2010 overtook Japan as the world's second-largest economy.

title: Soviet–Afghan War
summary: In December 1979 Soviet forces entered Afghanistan to prop up its communist government against rebel mujahideen, who were backed above all by Pakistan, the United States, the United Kingdom, China, Iran, Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states. Fighting raged through the 1980s, mostly in the countryside; the war killed an estimated one to three million Afghans and drove millions more to flee as refugees, mostly to Pakistan and Iran. The Soviet Union, which lost an estimated 14,453 to 26,000 soldiers, withdrew in February 1989.
why: The war added to the strains on the Soviet Union in its final years, and in Afghanistan fighting continued after the withdrawal until the Taliban seized Kabul and most of the country in 1996.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dissolution of the Soviet Union

title: The World Wide Web
summary: In March 1989 Tim Berners-Lee, an English computer scientist at the CERN physics laboratory, proposed a decentralised hypertext system for sharing information. By the end of 1990 he had a working browser, WorldWideWeb, and the first web server; the Web was released to other research institutions in January 1991 and to the whole Internet in August 1991, and on 30 April 1993 CERN made its protocols and code available royalty-free.
why: After the Mosaic browser appeared later in 1993, thousands of websites sprang up within a year, setting off the Web's explosive growth into a global information system.

title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
summary: Amid the revolutions sweeping the Eastern Bloc in 1989, an East German press conference on 9 November prematurely announced that East Germans could travel freely; crowds gathered at Berlin's crossings, and that night puzzled border guards let them through as the world watched on live television. Communist governments fell across Central and Eastern Europe that year, and Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990.
why: The fall of the Wall became a symbol of the collapse of communist rule in Europe and the end of the Cold War.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Fall of the Berlin Wall

title: Dissolution of the Soviet Union
summary: Economic stagnation, the burden of the arms race and foreign wars, nationalist movements in the union republics and the destabilising effects of Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms (glasnost and perestroika) eroded Soviet power. On 8 December 1991 the leaders of Russia, Belarus and Ukraine declared in the Belovezha Accords that the Soviet Union no longer existed; Gorbachev resigned on 25 December, and on 26 December 1991 the USSR was formally dissolved.
why: Fifteen independent states replaced the Soviet Union, with Russia as its recognised successor, ending the Cold War world of two rival superpowers.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dissolution of the Soviet Union

title: End of apartheid
summary: From 1948 South Africa's white-minority government enforced apartheid, a system of institutionalised racial segregation. In February 1990 President F. W. de Klerk announced the repeal of discriminatory laws and lifted the ban on anti-apartheid groups, and that year released Nelson Mandela after 27 years in prison; negotiations led to the country's first elections open to citizens of all races on 26–29 April 1994, won by Mandela's African National Congress with about 62 percent of the vote.
why: Mandela's inauguration on 10 May 1994 as South Africa's first Black president, heading a Government of National Unity, ended minority rule; he and de Klerk shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize for ending apartheid peacefully.

sources.title: Nobel Prize: The Nobel Peace Prize 1993

title: 9/11 and the war in Afghanistan
place: World Trade Center, New York City
summary: On 11 September 2001, 19 hijackers from the Islamist terrorist organisation al-Qaeda flew airliners into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon near Washington; a fourth plane crashed in Pennsylvania after its passengers fought back. The attacks killed 2,977 people. When Afghanistan's Taliban government refused to hand over al-Qaeda's leader Osama bin Laden, a US-led coalition invaded and toppled it, but the Taliban regrouped as an insurgency; after a US–Taliban deal in February 2020 and the withdrawal of US forces, the Taliban captured Kabul on 15 August 2021, and the last US military aircraft left on 30 August.
why: The 20-year war, the longest in US history, killed an estimated 176,000 to 212,000 or more people, including over 46,000 Afghan civilians, and ended with the Taliban's Islamic Emirate restored.

title: Global financial crisis
place: Lehman Brothers headquarters, Seventh Avenue, New York City
summary: A US housing boom fuelled by risky subprime mortgages turned to bust, and from early 2007 securities tied to those loans collapsed in value, spreading losses through banks worldwide. The crisis peaked when the investment bank Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on 15 September 2008, the largest bankruptcy in US history, triggering stock-market crashes and bank runs; governments responded with huge bank bailouts and monetary and fiscal stimulus to prevent a collapse of the financial system.
why: It deepened the Great Recession (December 2007 to June 2009), the longest US downturn since World War II, in which US unemployment peaked at 10 percent, and contributed to crises in Iceland and the eurozone.

sources.title: Federal Reserve History: The Great Recession

title: COVID-19 pandemic
summary: A new coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2, was first identified in an outbreak in Wuhan, China, in December 2019 and spread worldwide in early 2020; the World Health Organization (WHO) declared a public health emergency on 30 January and described the outbreak as a pandemic on 11 March 2020. Lockdowns, travel restrictions, school closures and remote working transformed daily life, vaccines were rolled out from December 2020, and the WHO declared the global health emergency over in May 2023.
why: About 7 million deaths were officially reported, but the WHO estimated 14.9 million excess deaths in 2020 and 2021 alone, and other estimates put the toll at 19 to 36 million; the pandemic also caused the largest global recession since the Great Depression.
